title: Evaluating Information Gathering Abilities of Large Language Models with QuestBench

contributions.purpose: Provide a rigorous, well-defined way to evaluate LLMs' ability to identify missing information under underspecification (rather than semantic ambiguity), by asking the minimally sufficient clarifying question.
contributions.mechanism: A constraint satisfaction (CSP) framework that formalizes underspecified reasoning tasks as CSPs with missing variable assignments; each task is a '1-sufficient CSP' where acquiring exactly one variable's value determines the target, framed as multiple-choice question selection.
contributions.evaluation: Definitional/formal framework (Known predicate, 1-sufficient CSP definitions); no quantitative metric, enables the downstream benchmark and difficulty metrics (search depth/width).
contributions.source_quote: Our contributions include (1) a constraint satisfaction framework enabling focused evaluation of un-derspecification in LLMs

contributions.purpose: Give the community a benchmark to measure whether LLMs can ask the right question to acquire missing information in reasoning tasks.
contributions.mechanism: QuestBench: a multiple-choice dataset spanning three domains built as 1-sufficient CSPs: Logic-Q (SimpleLogic-based logical reasoning with one missing proposition), Planning-Q (PDDL/Blocks World planning with partially observed initial state), and GSM-Q (grade-school math with one missing variable, constructed via human annotation from GSM-Plus distractor problems).
contributions.evaluation: Three-domain benchmark (Logic-Q, Planning-Q, GSM-Q) with tasks stratified by CSP difficulty (search depth, number of variables/constraints); dataset statistics in Table 1.
contributions.source_quote: Our contributions include ... (2) a benchmark QUESTBENCH for evaluating the information gathering abilities of LLMs

contributions.purpose: Characterize how well state-of-the-art LLMs perform at identifying missing information and diagnose what makes tasks hard for them.
contributions.mechanism: Empirical evaluation of Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, and GPT-4-o1 in zero-shot/few-shot/CoT settings; correlation analysis between LLM accuracy and CSP solver difficulty metrics (backward search depth, number of variables/constraints, brute-force guesses).
contributions.evaluation: Gemini/GPT-4o achieve ~15-44% (Logic-Q) and ~9-41% (Planning-Q); overall 20-30% zero/few-shot. GPT-4-o1 only 41-44% on a 100-sample subset despite 200-300x more inference tokens. GSM-Q is easy (Gemini Flash + CoT reaches ~90%). Accuracy negatively correlated with solver runtime complexity (statistically significant for most LLMs in Logic-Q).
contributions.source_quote: Our contributions include ... (3) empirical evaluation and analyses of LLM performance on QUESTBENCH. ... Our analyses reveal a negative correlation between LLM accuracy and solver runtime complexity, sug-gesting that LLMs may share similar limitations to CSP solvers.

self_declared_provenance.quote: We construct underspecified grade-school math problems from GSM-Plus' "distractor" setting (Li et al., 2024a), which was derived from adding a single distractor sentence to math problems in GSM8k (Cobbe et al., 2021)
SimpleLogic is a simple, fully synthetic setting to arbitrarily generate any logic problems.

notes: Benchmark paper reporting predominantly negative results about LLMs (a project signal): SOTA models only reach 20-30% overall and even reasoning-optimized GPT-4-o1 caps at ~40-44% on Logic-Q/Planning-Q. Notable caveat/near-null finding on GSM-Q: it is 'sufficiently easy' (up to ~90% with CoT) because construction reduced it to missing-variable detection; only 25% of GSM-Q problems had extraneous irrelevant variables, so authors caveat that GSM-Q may not test the intended skill. Planning-Q correlations with search metrics are weak/mixed (GPT-4-o1 even positively correlated), suggesting LLMs use non-search mechanisms there. Authors state limitation: only single-missing-piece tasks, unlike real multi-piece/ambiguous queries.
